title: Pagganck / Governors Island
summary: Pagganck is the name recorded for modern Governors Island in a June 16, 1637 deed. The record names Cacapeteyno and Pewihas as owners acting with the consent of their community at Keshaechquereren and conveys the island to Wouter van Twiller. Later sources also preserve the spelling Pagganch.
address_label: Governors Island, New York Harbor, New York, NY (historic northern island footprint)
map_geometry_source: Approximate public point near Fort Jay on the historic northern/original footprint of Governors Island. A point is used instead of the modern island polygon because the southern 103 acres were added with fill in the early twentieth century.
introduction_content: Pagganck is a recorded Indigenous place name for the island now called Governors Island. The Dutch later called it Nooten or Nutten Island, preserving a related nut-island association in colonial naming.
history_content: Land Papers GG 17 records that on June 16, 1637, Cacapeteyno and Pewihas appeared as owners acting by order of their leaders and with the consent of the community at Keshaechquereren. The document says they conveyed to Wouter van Twiller “Nut Island, in the Indian tongue called Pagganck,” opposite Manhattan. This colonial deed is evidence of the recorded name and of a colonial land transfer; it should not be read as a complete account of Native relationships to the island or as proof that colonial and Indigenous understandings of landholding were identical.
translation_content: The 1637 record spells the name Pagganck. William Wallace Tooker also noted the form Pagganch. Tooker compared the word with terms for walnut and other hard-shell nuts and concluded that it was probably related to “nut trees,” while explicitly acknowledging that the translation was an interpretation rather than a certainty.
preservation_content: Governors Island was substantially enlarged in the early twentieth century. This listing therefore uses a point on the older northern island rather than presenting the full modern shoreline as the seventeenth-century landform.
whereintheworld_content: Pagganck is modern Governors Island in New York Harbor, south of Manhattan and west of Brooklyn. The marker is placed on the historic northern footprint near Fort Jay.
